client: I've been really struggling since I started this new job at the tech startup — the pace is just relentless and I feel like I'm constantly behind. Last week I missed an important deadline, and I can't stop replaying it in my head, wondering what my manager and coworkers think of me now. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is still going to be there when I walk out of here.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — the relentless pace, the missed deadline, and this loop of worry about what others think of you. I also notice that even as you're describing all this pressure, there's a part of you that seems to be holding back a little, almost like you're bracing yourself or not fully sure it's safe to let it all out here. What would it mean for you if talking about this *could* actually help, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I guess... part of me is skeptical that talking about it actually changes anything, you know? Like, the deadline is still missed, my manager still probably thinks I'm unreliable, and no amount of talking is going to undo that. But I'll admit there's something kind of exhausting about carrying it around alone, so maybe that's what you mean by it helping "a little."
therapist: That moment of recognition — that carrying it alone is exhausting — feels really important, and I don't want to gloss over it. Even if talking can't undo the missed deadline, it can help us loosen the grip of that mental replay and examine whether your mind is telling you the full, accurate story about what your manager thinks of you. What does that inner critic actually *say* to you when the replay kicks in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It says things like "you're incompetent" and "everyone can see you're not cut out for this job" — and once it starts, it just snowballs. Like, one missed deadline becomes proof that I've been faking my way through everything all along. I know that sounds extreme when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: What you just described — one mistake becoming "proof" of everything you feared about yourself — is a really classic thinking pattern called overgeneralization, and the fact that you can already notice it sounds extreme is actually a meaningful crack of light. But I'm also picking up that even as you're describing it somewhat analytically, there's a real urgency and distress underneath — like your body is still *in* that moment even as your words try to make sense of it. When that snowball starts rolling, where do you feel it first — is it more in your thoughts, or does it show up somewhere in your body too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, it's... honestly both, but the body stuff hits first. Like before I even have a coherent thought about what went wrong, there's this tightening in my chest and my stomach just drops, like I'm falling. And then my brain kind of scrambles to catch up and explain why I feel that way, and that's when the story starts — "see, this is who you are, this is what you do."
therapist: What you're describing is such a key insight — your body is actually *leading* the story, not just reacting to it, and then your mind rushes in to explain the alarm with the harshest possible narrative. In CBT we'd call that emotional reasoning, where the feeling becomes the evidence: "I feel like a fraud, therefore I must be one." So one thing we can start to explore together is whether we can interrupt that chain earlier — what do you notice about that chest tightening in the moment, and have you ever been able to pause there before the story takes over?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean, yeah, I can kind of see what you're saying about the feeling coming first... but honestly, by the time I even notice the chest tightening, the story is already running at full speed. It's like I don't get a warning — one second I'm fine, and the next I'm already convinced everyone in the room can see right through me. I'm not sure I'd even know how to pause there, because it happens so fast it doesn't feel like there's a gap to step into.
therapist: The speed you're describing is real — it genuinely can feel like there's no gap, but what's actually happening is that the gap is there, it's just very small and your nervous system has gotten very practiced at sprinting through it. What's interesting is that even right now, as you're describing feeling like there's no way in, your voice has a kind of energy to it that makes me wonder if part of you is actually more engaged with finding that gap than you're giving yourself credit for. What if the goal wasn't to stop the story, but just to notice, even one second after it starts, "oh, there it is again" — do you think that tiny shift might feel any different?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... maybe, I guess. Like, I hear what you're saying about the gap being there, but honestly, by the time I even realize I'm in the spiral, I'm already like ten steps deep into convincing myself that everyone at work thinks I'm incompetent or that I messed up that email or whatever. I don't know if "oh, there it is again" is going to feel like anything other than just another thought getting swallowed up by the rest of them.
therapist: That fear — that even the awareness itself just becomes another drop in the flood — makes a lot of sense, and I don't want to oversell a simple phrase as a magic fix. What I'm noticing though is that you've actually been catching yourself throughout our whole conversation: "I know that sounds extreme," "the feeling comes first," and just now, "I'm already ten steps deep" — that *is* the noticing, happening in real time. What if the skill you're worried you don't have is actually something you're already doing, just not yet giving yourself credit for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it also feels like there's a difference between noticing something out loud when someone's asking me questions and actually catching it in the moment when I'm alone at two in the morning and the spiral is already happening. Like, here it feels safer, more controlled, so of course I can do it here. I'm just not convinced that translates to when I'm really in it.
therapist: You're making a really honest and important distinction — what feels possible in a safe, structured conversation and what feels possible at 2am when you're alone and the walls are closing in are genuinely different challenges, and I don't want to flatten that. But I'm also noticing something in how you said that — there's a kind of quiet weight to it, like this isn't just a hypothetical "2am," like you might know that feeling pretty specifically. How often are you actually finding yourself in that place at night?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, you're right, it's not hypothetical. I'd say it happens maybe three or four nights a week where I'm just lying there and it gets really loud in my head, all the guilt and the replaying of things, and the silence in the apartment just makes it worse somehow. It's like the loneliness has more room to expand at night when there's nothing to distract from it.
therapist: Three or four nights a week is a lot of nights to be alone with that kind of noise, and the way you described the loneliness having "more room to expand" — that's a really vivid and tender way to put it, and it tells me this goes beyond just work stress. I want to make sure I'm hearing the full picture: when you're in that place at 2am, with the guilt and the replaying and the silence, what does that feel like for you emotionally — is it more like anxiety, or does it tip into something that feels closer to sadness or hopelessness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's kind of both, but if I had to pick one word it would be... hollow. Like, the anxiety is there at the start, the replaying and the "what if I'd said this instead" loop, but then somewhere around 2 or 3am it shifts into something quieter and heavier, where I'm not even really thinking anymore, I'm just sort of... existing in this gray feeling. It's not quite hopelessness, because I wake up and I function, but in those moments it genuinely feels like I don't matter much to anyone, and that thought just sits there.
therapist: That word — "hollow" — lands really heavily, and I want to sit with it for a moment rather than move past it, because "I don't matter much to anyone" is a painful thought to carry alone in the dark three or four nights a week. I also notice you said it quite quickly, almost like you wanted to get it out before you thought too hard about it — and I'm wondering if that thought, that you don't matter, is one you've been holding for a while but haven't quite said out loud before. When did that feeling first start showing up for you — was it with this job, or does it feel older than that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, it's... it's older than the job. I think I've been carrying it since maybe college, when I realized I could disappear from a room and nobody would really notice or come looking for me. I just got good at convincing myself it wasn't true, staying busy, keeping moving — and now that I'm not as busy, there's nowhere to hide from it.
therapist: What you just shared feels like something really significant — like you've just named something you've been outrunning for a long time, and the job stress was almost just the thing that finally made you stop. The way you said that, quietly and quickly, makes me wonder if part of you is still a little afraid to let it fully land — like if you say it too slowly, it becomes too real. I want to ask you gently: that college-age version of you who could disappear from a room and nobody came looking — what did they need that they didn't get?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
